Privacy is less and less, but you have a certain degree of control of it.

 

GPS on your phone

As much as possible, disable it and/or review apps/process that require GPS location data. Most of them have opt-out options for sending data to them periodically.

IP address that can reveal a "real word location"

Yes, IP address can be traced by country assigned to it, ISP block, base-station location, etc. Use trusted VPN/VPS service if you want to bypass geo-restriction/leave less tracks.

3rd parties tracking your internet activities and collecting data - and then plugging it into algorithms to customize ads, etc.

Use adblock software by default and disabling it on sites you trust and want to support. Script blockers enabled and only turned off per site temporarily or permanent depending on what site it is. Ghostery and similar software to reduce data being tracked on you.

Research done on people's brains to identify high-yield marketing strategies, specifically tailored to exploit your mind's weak points/vulnerabilities

Nothing much you can do aside from being aware of it and being skeptical. Re-think your actions that have a possibility of a long term effect.

Classically, government surveillance. And/or corporate.

and

When scanning fingerprint on scanner, instead of lifting your finger after a scan, do a wipe down to smudge the oil that may have left that formed your fingerprint. Be wary of cameras and search for them when first entering a room, but not be too obvious on it. Minimize exposure, but being too obvious will raise more suspicion.

Aside from that, nothing much you can do.

New/er methods of IDing - eyes, hair, ears, idk what else. Biometrics and such.

I'd also love to hear from experts - what are ways in which our privacy is diminished when we're online? For example, there is data embedded in photos we post online, etc. Please inform us - what should we be aware of?

You can always be careful what you post online by not being too specific, like places visited with date, what your possible appearance is, etc. For the data embedded on photos, those are EXIF. Best practice before sharing an image online is to check if there's no identifiable information on it; remove exif data by simply copy/paste the image to mspaint/basic image editor and upload that instead.

Those are just some. Others may post more information.

I'm particularly interested in metadata - probably because here in Australia it is collected and shared indiscriminately.

I view the average internet user as "walking around naked and blind" (inb4 hurr durr). Naked because all our online/cellphone/location metadata is visible to effectively everyone (ISPs, telcos, all branches of government and everyone employed by them) and blind because it is not visible to us.

The metadata/surveillance genie is out of the bottle, now, and "privacy" will never be regained. In my view we should turn privacy on its head, and generally make our metadata public. This would make online activity more similar to irl activity - we can see each other walking down the street, looking in shop windows, visiting the doctor - but cannot listen in to conversations or know what ailment takes us to the doctor (because metadata is visible but data is not).

If I can see my friend's cellphone GPS metadata, for example, I might notice that they have usually gone to work at this time of the day - and if for the last couple of days they've stayed at home, I might call them to see if they're ok. This is what used to happen when we noticed our neighbour hasn't left their front door for a couple of days. Most of us "who have nothing to hide" need not fear this.

We would still be naked - but maybe we wouldn't be quite as blind.

Of course privacy exists, you just have to choose to participate in it. You choose what to share on Facebook, you choose to use the World Wide Web via HTTP protocol, you choose what phone you carry. You choose which car to buy, etc.

Privacy is definitely going out the door, on all levels. There was this article about a chimpanzee controlling a mechanical arm with its thoughts. Here's a link. http://www.nytimes.com/2008/05/29/science/29brain.html?_r=0 The implications are huge. A sensor was used to translate a thought into an action. Very cool applications to that technology. But also very dangerous ones. A tool can be used for good or wrong, it all comes down to who is holding it. So back to the point, we were able to translate a chimp's thought into an action. Its only a matter of time until we translate a human thought into an action. It is literally reading one's mind. And its only a question of time until more powerful sensors are created. Until more thoughts can be read. So yeah, my opinion, forget about privacy.

Privacy still exists but it's endangered. It's really sad that this is what the world is becoming. Instead of having privacy, I'm afraid we as a collective are going to need to be more open minded to each others faults and fetishes, so we can't be controlled by this information. That's a pretty hard task, I hope we are all up for it.
